narration: Welcome to Mission Control — FactoryLM's central command interface for your industrial automation cluster. Here's everything it can do.
Chat Relay is the core of Mission Control. It routes natural language prompts directly to Claude Code running on any Jarvis node in your cluster.
This dropdown lets you target a specific machine — Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, or the VPS.
Choose how long to wait for a response: one, three, five, or ten minutes.
Type your prompt in this field — exactly what you'd type into Claude Code at the terminal. Control-Enter dispatches it.
Results appear in the message history below — expandable cards with stdout, stderr, exit code, and elapsed time.
The status indicator at the top right shows which Jarvis nodes are reachable in real time.
The Dashboard is your live system snapshot — everything happening across the cluster on a single screen.
Four stat cards show current workflow count, active worker pool size, agent count, and Ralph's live status.
The Human-in-the-Loop queue is where autonomous actions wait before executing. Each item is color-coded by risk — green for safe, yellow for caution, red for destructive.
Action types include deployments, git pushes, force-pushes, deletes, PLC writes, and repo resurrections. You approve or reject each one individually.
The right column shows every Jarvis node in the cluster and its current health status.
Below that, PLC collector status — S7, Allen-Bradley, and Modbus — shows whether live industrial telemetry is flowing.
Quick Actions let you fire common shell commands with one click. Each is tagged with a risk level so you know what you're touching before you hit it.
The Terminal tab gives you a direct remote shell into any Jarvis node without leaving the browser.
Pick your target node from the dropdown, then set a command timeout from ten seconds to two minutes.
The same Quick Actions grid is here for one-click access to preset commands.
Worker Swarm manages the Celery task pool that powers every autonomous operation in the cluster.
Workers are organized into eight categories: Core Operations, Knowledge, Analysis, Integration, PLC, Content, Development, and Security — twenty-five workers total.
Each card shows the worker's formatted name and live status — active, running, idle, or offline.
The plus and minus buttons grow or shrink the pool for any worker by one instance. Scale up under load, scale down to save resources.
Ralph is Mission Control's autonomous code evolution engine — it iterates on a codebase continuously, proposing and applying improvements in a loop.
The status badge tells you whether Ralph is running, paused, stopped, or has tripped an error state.
Stats track total iterations completed, the current session identifier, and the circuit breaker state.
You can start Ralph on any project path, then pause or stop mid-loop without losing state. Pause is non-destructive — it resumes exactly where it left off.
The circuit breaker auto-halts Ralph when failure count exceeds a configured threshold. The health bar shows your current failure ratio at a glance.
The safety warning is there for a reason — Ralph makes real changes to real code. Always point it at a feature branch, not main.
The Agents tab manages the four high-level autonomous agents that coordinate the entire worker layer.

Ralph handles code evolution. Cosmos runs the video production pipeline. MediaOffload handles media archival and compression. And Jesus H Christ is the repo resurrection specialist. Each agent can be started or stopped independently.
The Tools tab is where the monetized services live — starting with Jesus H Christ, Repo Resurrection.
JHC takes dead or abandoned GitHub repositories and brings them back to life — updated dependencies, repaired CI, and a working test suite.
To resurrect a specific repo, paste the URL and choose your aggression level.
Gentle is documentation-only work at ninety-nine dollars. Moderate handles dependencies and CI at two-ninety-nine. Full aggressive refactor — the complete overhaul — is nine-ninety-nine.
These checkboxes let you fine-tune what JHC is allowed to touch — dependency upgrades and CI configuration are controlled separately.
Every resurrection queues an approval action in the HIL queue first. Nothing touches your codebase until you say so.
Git Forensics runs static analysis on any local repository — full history reports and hotspot detection to find which files change most and why.
Finally, the Ladder Logic tab embeds a live reference view of the Micro 820 PLC's control program.
This is a direct window into the PLC logic — rungs, coils, and contacts — running live alongside your factory hardware.
That's Mission Control — eight tabs, forty-plus autonomous capabilities, one unified command surface for the entire FactoryLM cluster.
